item.text: {"text":"Large margins against random negatives do not establish strong catalog ranking. Dallmann et al. found that both uniform and popularity-sampled evaluation can reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog evaluation ([study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13045)). Prakash et al. (2024) compared six negative-sampling approaches across three sequential-recommendation datasets: aggregate metrics concealed head/mid/tail disparities; random sampling favored head items, while popularity-based sampling sometimes improved balance at an overall accuracy cost ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)). Recent sampling research also emphasizes false negatives: difficult unobserved items may be relevant, so hardness alone does not justify treating them as dislikes ([survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07237)).\n\nPractical diagnostic implication: freeze separate candidate panels containing uniformly sampled unseen items, popularity-matched alternatives, title/description neighbors, and the trained model’s highest-scoring unseen items. Use local TF-IDF similarity for text panels without external weights. Report positive-rank distributions, positive-minus-maximum-candidate margins, and the fraction of alternatives outranking the observed positive; stratify by training-only item-frequency bands and user-history length, with counts and uncertainty. Compare equally sized panels to isolate candidate difficulty; report full-catalog ranks separately where affordable. These are proposed stress tests, not established benchmark replacements. Keep the pinned host evaluator and macro validation HR@10 unchanged, label every diagnostic by its candidate construction, and interpret outranking unseen items as ambiguity or competition rather than confirmed recommendation errors."}
